stem: An investigator measures the time required for complete genome replication in Escherichia coli and in cultured human cells.  The human genome is approximately 1,000 times larger, but replication takes only about 10 times as long.  Which of the following features of eukaryotic DNA replication best accounts for this finding?​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​‌​​​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌​​​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​

options.text: Bidirectional fork progression from each origin

options.label: B
options.text: Continuous synthesis of the lagging strand

options.label: D
options.text: Multiple DNA polymerases with distinct functions

explanation:
D NA replication follows the same basic sequence in prokaryotes (eg, Escherichia coli) and eukaryotes: the double helix is unwound by helicase to form a replication fork, primase lays down RNA primers, DNA polymerases synthesize and proofread the daughter strands, the primers are replaced with DNA, and ligase seals the Okazaki fragments of the lagging strand.

However, the genomes themselves differ substantially.  The prokaryotic genome is a single small circular chromosome that is replicated continuously as the cell grows.  In contrast, the eukaryotic genome is far larger, packaged into chromatin, distributed across multiple linear chromosomes, and replicated only during S phase of the cell cycle.  Because each chromosome is a separate DNA molecule, replication cannot proceed onto it from an origin located elsewhere, and each chromosome is individually far longer than the entire prokaryotic genome.

The eukaryotic genome therefore contains tens of thousands of replication initiation sites (ie, origins of replication), whereas the entire prokaryotic genome has only one.  During S phase, origins are activated at successive times across the genome, dividing it into many short segments that are replicated in parallel.  Because total replication time depends on the length each fork must travel rather than on genome size alone, this parallelism allows the entire genome to be duplicated within a single S phase.

(Choice A)  Replication is bidirectional in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes; two forks form at each origin and progress in opposite directions.  Because this feature is shared, it cannot account for the difference between the two systems.

(Choice B)  DNA polymerases synthesize only in the 5′→3′ direction in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes.  Consequently, the lagging strand is always synthesized discontinuously as Okazaki fragments, which are subsequently joined by ligase.

(Choice C)  Helicase hydrolyzes ATP to separate the DNA strands in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes; unwinding is energy dependent in each.

(Choice D)  Eukaryotes have more DNA polymerases with specialized roles (α, β, γ, δ, ε) than prokaryotes (I, II, III).  However, these enzymes divide the labor of replication and repair rather than accelerate it; eukaryotic replication forks actually advance more slowly than prokaryotic forks, in part because chromatin must be disassembled and reassembled as the fork passes.

Educational objective:The prokaryotic genome has a single origin of replication, whereas the eukaryotic genome has tens of thousands.  Activating numerous origins allows the much larger eukaryotic genome to be replicated in parallel and completed within a single S phase.​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​‌​​​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌​​​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​
